etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English cruel, borrowed from Old French cruel, from Latin crūdēlis (“hard, severe, cruel”), akin to crūdus (“raw, crude”); see crude.

definitions.definition: Intentionally causing or reveling in pain and suffering; merciless, heartless.

quote.citation: 2013, Ranulph Fiennes, Cold: Extreme Adventures at the Lowest Temperatures on Earth:
quote.text: He was physically the toughest of us and wore five layers of polar clothing, but the cold was cruel and wore us down hour after hour.

quote.citation: 1951, C. S. Lewis, Prince Caspian: The Return to Narnia:
quote.text: You may be sure they watched the cliffs on their left eagerly for any sign of a break or any place where they could climb them; but those cliffs remained cruel.

quote.citation: 1913, Arthur Conan Doyle, “(please specify the page)”, in The Poison Belt […], London; New York, N.Y.: Hodder and Stoughton, →OCLC:
quote.text: "But I've served 'im ten years, and I'm fond of 'im, and, mind you, 'e's a great man, when all's said an' done, and it's an honor to serve 'im. But 'e does try one cruel at times."

quote.citation: 2016, Kerry Greenwood, Murder and Mendelssohn, Sydney: Allen and Unwin, page 219:
quote.text: 'I've never got arthritis, though my old dad had it something cruel.'

definitions.definition: (chiefly Australia, New Zealand) To spoil or ruin (one's chance of success)

quote.citation: 1937, Vance Palmer, Legend for Sanderson‎[1], Sydney: Angus & Robertson, page 226:
quote.text: What cruelled him was that Imperial Hotel contract.
He was on the fringes of Test selection last year before a shoulder injury cruelled his chances.

A shortage of berth space for mega container ships will restrict capacity at Melbourne's port, cruelling Labor's attempts to get maximum value from its privatisation, a leading shipping expert has warned.

definitions.definition: (Australia, transitive, intransitive) To violently provoke (a child) in the belief that this will make them more assertive.

quote.citation: 2007, Stewart Motha, “Reconciliation as Domination”, in Scott Veitch, editor, Law and the Politics of Reconciliation‎[2], Routledge, published 2016, page 83:
quote.text: Violence is apparently introduced early by the practice of "cruelling": children even in their first months are physically punished and then encouraged to seek retribution by punishing the punisher.

quote.citation: 2009, Mark Colvin, ABC, "Peter Sutton discusses the politics of suffering in Aboriginal communities," 2 July, 2009, [3]
quote.text: […]  I was referring to the area where you were talking about this practice of cruelling; the pinching of babies, sometimes so hard that their skin breaks and may go septic.
